english: Let $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ be defined by $f(x)=\sin\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)+\cos\left(\sin\dfrac{2\pi x}{3}\right)$. Then the fundamental period of $f$ is
hindi: माना कि $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, $f(x)=\sin\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)+\cos\left(\sin\dfrac{2\pi x}{3}\right)$ द्वारा परिभाषित है। तब $f$ का मूल आवर्तकाल है
solution: $\sin(\cos(t+\pi))=\sin(-\cos t)=-\sin(\cos t)$, so $\sin(\cos t)$ has fundamental period $2\pi$ (not $\pi$); with $t=\dfrac{\pi x}{2}$: period $4$
$\cos(\sin(t+\pi))=\cos(-\sin t)=\cos(\sin t)$, and no smaller shift works, so $\cos(\sin t)$ has period $\pi$; with $t=\dfrac{2\pi x}{3}$: period $\dfrac32$

Check: $f(x+6)=-\sin\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)+\cos\left(\sin\dfrac{2\pi x}{3}\right)\ne f(x)$ (at $x=0$: $1-\sin1\ne1+\sin1$), so $6$ is not a period ($6$ comes from taking $\pi$ as the period of $\sin(\cos t)$)
solution_full: First term $u(x)=\sin\left(\cos\dfrac{\pi x}{2}\right)$. Put $t=\dfrac{\pi x}{2}$. Since $\cos(t+\pi)=-\cos t$ and $\sin$ is odd, $\sin(\cos(t+\pi))=-\sin(\cos t)$, which is not identically equal to $\sin(\cos t)$ (at $t=0$ the values are $-\sin1$ and $\sin1$). Since $\cos t$ has fundamental period $2\pi$ and $\sin$ is one-one on $[-1,1]$, the fundamental period of $\sin(\cos t)$ is $2\pi$; in $x$ it is $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/2}=4$.

Second term $v(x)=\cos\left(\sin\dfrac{2\pi x}{3}\right)$. Put $s=\dfrac{2\pi x}{3}$. Since $\sin(s+\pi)=-\sin s$ and $\cos$ is even, $\cos(\sin(s+\pi))=\cos(\sin s)$. As $\cos$ is one-one on $[0,1]$, $\cos(\sin s)$ repeats exactly when $|\sin s|$ repeats, whose fundamental period is $\pi$. In $x$ the period is $\dfrac{\pi}{2\pi/3}=\dfrac32$.

The periods $4$ and $\dfrac32$ are commensurable, with $\dfrac{4}{3/2}=\dfrac83$ in lowest terms, so the period of $f=u+v$ is their LCM: $\dfrac{\mathrm{LCM}(8,3)}{\mathrm{HCF}(2,2)}=\dfrac{24}{2}=12$; indeed $12=3\cdot4=8\cdot\dfrac32$.

No proper divisor of the form $\dfrac{12}{k}$ works. For example $f(x+6)=-u(x)+v(x)$, which differs from $f(x)$ at $x=0$; and $f(x+4)=u(x)+\cos\left(\sin\left(\dfrac{2\pi x}{3}+\dfrac{8\pi}{3}\right)\right)$, which at $x=0$ equals $\sin1+\cos\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\ne\sin1+1$. A numerical scan of all shifts $T\in(0,12)$ confirms that $12$ is the least period.
Option (A) results from taking $\pi$ as the period of $\sin(\cos t)$, and (C) is the period of the first term alone.
originality_note: New: a sum of the two mirror composites sin(cos) and cos(sin) with different inner frequencies, chosen so that the classic slip (both having period pi) changes the answer from 12 to 6 (way 5). Closest known: period of sin(cos x) or cos(sin x) alone, and of |sin x|+|cos x|. Different because: the two composites behave differently under a half-period shift and the sum's LCM must be formed with a fractional period.

concept_use.Period of a sum, product or composite of: The period of the sum is the LCM of 4 and 3/2, which is 12.
concept_use.Periodic functions: fundamental period: The fundamental periods of sin(cos t) (2 pi) and cos(sin t) (pi) are established, and 12 is checked to be the least period (6 and 4 fail).

stem_review: Read as a student: f defined with domain; 'fundamental period' is standard. Numerical scan of shifts in (0,12) found no smaller period; f(x+12)=f(x) to 1e-14. Options all numbers; plan D. Changed: No change.
key_step: Recognising that sin(cos t) has period 2 pi while cos(sin t) has period pi, then taking LCM(4, 3/2).
justification: Routine multi-step chain: two composite periods plus an LCM with a fractional period; the trap is a familiar one. Comparable to 2024-P1-Q3 (L3 trig evaluation) on the lower side and to routine L2 period questions; below 2026-P1-Q14 (L3).
blueprint_concepts: Period of a sum, product or composite of periodic functions
